analysis.title: CIO Special | 10 themes for the year ahead
key_insights: DWS's fourth annual list of 10 medium-term themes. Geopolitics, AI and monetary policy are the main drivers, and the CIO says the US attack on Iran in February raised energy costs, inflation and interest rates worldwide.

Theme 1: DWS expects US-Europe tensions to leave the transatlantic alliance stronger and less transactional, citing the Brexit precedent. Cross-border investment ties are deep: about 60% of US foreign direct investment goes to Europe.

Theme 2: Emerging and developing economies are 61% of global GDP on a PPP basis. The IMF expects them to grow 3.8% in 2026 versus 1.7% for advanced economies. DWS says country and sector selection matter more than headline GDP growth and does not recommend indiscriminate EM exposure.

Theme 3: DWS argues the era of cheap money is ending under Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who has been in office since May. The open question is where long-term yields settle, with deficits, elevated issuance and term premium keeping upward pressure on the long end. The 30-year Treasury yield at 5.5% is a multi-decade high.

Theme 3: Long-duration, high-valuation assets look most vulnerable to higher yields. Companies with stable cash flows, strong balance sheets and pricing power look more resilient, and credit dispersion is expected to widen.

Theme 4: Germany's new Altersvorsorgedepot retirement account starts in 2027 and allows investment without a capital guarantee. A proposed funded pillar of 2% additional contributions, about EUR 35bn a year, is still under discussion. Germany is over 4% of global output but about 1% of global pension assets.

Theme 5: DWS is constructive on European equities through its 'New Europe' grouping of industrials, banks, semiconductors and utilities. These sectors are about 40% of the Stoxx Europe 600, up from about 25% in 2015, and their earnings have grown faster than autos, chemicals and consumer goods.

Theme 5: The S&P 500's top ten stocks are nearly 40% of the index, about twice the Stoxx Europe 600's top-ten share. Tech is over 50% of S&P 500 earnings. DWS expects European earnings growth to return to double digits in 2026 and 2027, and says 55% of Stoxx Europe 600 revenue comes from outside Europe.

Theme 6: AI agents are driving token usage and compute demand. Chipmakers are positioned at supply-chain bottlenecks and their free cash flow is forecast to rise sharply through 2028, while hyperscalers are moving from asset-light to capital-intensive and increasingly rely on external financing.

Theme 6: DWS expects AI leadership to broaden from semiconductors toward cloud, software and cybersecurity. It notes that as of 10/19/26 the SOX is down 24% and the KOSPI down 39% from their June highs.

Theme 7: Market concentration is high. The top market-cap decile held 78% of US equity value in July 2026, while the number of companies in that decile fell to 165. DWS lists four AI risks: weak returns on spending, valuations that depend on demanding profit forecasts, rising financing costs, and today's winners not capturing the value.

Theme 7: DWS recommends diversification by economic driver, not holding count. It separates AI financers from AI spending beneficiaries, favors structural trends such as grid investment, automation and cybersecurity, and says government bonds hedge disinflationary shocks while energy, infrastructure and real assets hedge inflationary ones.

Theme 8: US population growth is at its lowest in over a century, so growth leans on productivity. DWS sees industrial, service-oriented retail and higher-quality residential real estate as relatively well positioned and non-prime offices as structurally challenged. Renting has a cost advantage over buying.

Theme 9: Water scarcity is becoming a constraint on trade, industry, data centers, chip fabrication and mining. DWS expects water to be repriced, with opportunities in risk identification and in solutions such as treatment, recycling, leakage reduction and desalination.

Theme 10: Falling launch costs from reusable rockets could make space an infrastructure layer. The beneficiary set includes satellite operators, communications and Earth-observation firms, defense contractors and chipmakers, but orbital data centers are more relevant in the 2030s and 2040s.

sector_views.rationale: DWS calls these the 'New Europe' sectors it likes most, driven by electrification, defense, infrastructure and consolidation, with earnings growing faster than traditional sectors.
'Old Europe' sectors have had slower earnings growth as the key growth drivers change.
Slower working-age population growth and AI reshaping office jobs limit demand outside prime locations.

sector_views.sector: US industrial, service-oriented retail and higher-quality residential real estate
sector_views.rationale: E-commerce, data-center demand, service tenants and household formation support demand.
Strong earnings and free cash flow at AI bottlenecks, but semiconductor-heavy indices are down more than 20% from June peaks and valuations depend on demanding profit forecasts.
DWS expects tech leadership to broaden toward the application layer as AI agents spread.

earnings_insights: DWS expects average European earnings growth to return to double digits in 2026 and 2027 after three years of stagnation (forecast).

Consensus estimates point to a sharp rise in free cash flow for five semiconductor companies (Nvidia, TSMC, Broadcom, Micron, AMD) through 2028E, ahead of five hyperscalers (Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle) (consensus forecast).
Forward 12-month S&P 500 earnings are nearly 90% above the 10-year cyclically adjusted earnings base, near the top of the historical range (forward estimate basis).

macro_indicators.indicator: Emerging and developing economies GDP growth
macro_indicators.interpretation: IMF forecast from the July 2026 update, well above the 1.7% expected for advanced economies.
IMF forecast from the July 2026 update, below emerging market growth.
The chart marks it as a multi-decade high, supporting DWS's view of structurally higher capital costs.
Modest, so the international revenue reach of European companies matters more.

macro_indicators.indicator: Top market-cap decile share of US equity value
macro_indicators.interpretation: Close to the upper end of the long-run range, showing high concentration.

risk_factors: Higher yields from larger deficits, inflation and term premium could pressure consumers, businesses and valuations.
The AI capex cycle may not generate enough revenue or productivity to justify its cost, and it contributes to inflation.
Semiconductor valuations look affordable on forward multiples but could become expensive if earnings disappoint.
AI financing needs could raise borrowing costs for technology companies, utilities and suppliers, and hyperscalers rely increasingly on debt.
Today's perceived AI winners may not capture the long-term value.
Chair Warsh specifically called out record new issuance, demand and tight credit spreads.
Water stress could curtail facilities in water-scarce regions such as Arizona.
Space business models depend on reusable rockets, funding and regulatory approvals.
charts_described: US direct investment position by region in 2025: Europe at USD 4,300bn foreign direct investment in the US versus USD 3,729bn US direct investment abroad.
30-year US Treasury yield chart annotated '5.5% yield marks multi-decade high', plotted against US debt as a % of GDP with a CBO projection.
Water withdrawn during electricity generation, in liters per MWh: wind and solar PV under 10 and 100, gas CCGT 750, coal 2,540, nuclear 2,600.
Launch cost to low Earth orbit: $20,000/kg legacy, $1,500/kg reusable rockets today, $200/kg mid-2030s potential, on a log scale.
vol_and_positioning: Equity market concentration is high: the S&P 500's top ten stocks are nearly 40% of the index, and the top US market-cap decile holds 78% of aggregate value across 165 companies.
As of 10/19/26 the SOX is down 24% and the KOSPI down 39% from their June highs.
geopolitical: The US attack on Iran in February raised global energy costs, inflation and interest rates, and the US course and way out remain unclear.
Trump's America First policies and transatlantic tensions, which DWS expects to end in a stronger alliance.
The shift in global centers of power and alliances, including the question of which major power emerging markets will orient toward.
US-China technological competition expected to accelerate investment in space, communications, defense and computing.
Europe's push for strategic autonomy and rising defense and infrastructure spending.
cross_bank_references: BofA Global Research is cited for the launch-cost chart in Theme 10 and for the note 'Is AI momentum starting to cool?' in Theme 5.

tension_points.bull_case: Markets have absorbed higher yields better than expected, and AI productivity gains could offset part of the rise in capital costs.
tension_points.bear_case: Yields driven by deficits, inflation and term premium would pressure consumers, businesses and valuations, and the AI investment cycle may be vulnerable to tighter financial conditions.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Returns from the real economy failing to grow faster than the cost of capital.

tension_points.bull_case: Agentic AI is boosting token and compute demand, and chip companies are generating strong earnings and free cash flow.
tension_points.bear_case: Hyperscalers are becoming capital-intensive and dependent on external financing, and the entities supplying the buildout may not be the ones earning durable returns.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Hyperscaler cash flows failing to recover as AI and cloud revenues grow.

theme_stances.key_argument: Deficits, elevated issuance and higher term premium may keep yields above the levels of the previous decade.
theme_stances.evidence: Several factors could keep yields above the exceptionally low levels

theme_stances.key_argument: Industrials, banks, semiconductors and utilities are gaining index weight and growing earnings faster than traditional sectors.
theme_stances.evidence: we remain constructive on European equities

theme_stances.key_argument: Chip companies sit at supply-chain bottlenecks and earn higher margins and free cash flow than hyperscalers.
theme_stances.evidence: those sitting at bottlenecks will tend to have higher margins
